title: the key operations of the lifecycle review: files the services read, the TPM credential, a staged pid-map key

findings.claim: LR-3: rotate-kek run as root left kek.json, every wrapped key and the runtime KEK root's (0600), so the services (the secrets folder's owner) opened no key; fixed: each file is given to the folder's owner before it takes its name

LR-4: unseal after a restart (the runbook's step and the installer's re-run) left the runtime KEK and the folder it made root's, and an unreadable KEK was a bare PermissionError custody() did not catch; fixed: both are the services', the folder 0700, an unreadable KEK is a KekError

LR-6: rotate-kek --backend file on a TPM box left the credential sealing the old KEK; fixed: the new KEK is sealed beside it and opened again before the commit, the credential is swapped first in the roll-forward, no systemd-creds is refused before any change

LR-7: rotate-kek wrote over and renamed away the key an interrupted rotate pid_map staged under the same name; fixed: rotate-kek refuses a staged key it did not journal, rotate pid_map takes the folder's lock and waits for a KEK rotation cut short

rotate-kek from a TPM box to the passphrase, shamir or kms back end leaves the credential and the boot unit on the old KEK: each boot writes the old KEK to /run/trialbox/kek and the services refuse it (no key is lost)
unseal hands over only a runtime folder it makes; a folder already there, root's and 0700, stays closed to the services until seal_keys.sh's hand-over runs
the runtime KEK's place still comes from --out or TB_KEK_FILE in the caller's environment (unseal, rotate-kek); the card's rule says no caller's variable decides where a secret goes

LR-3's read-only class: restic-key, wrap and the audit signing key write through store_key and now get the folder's owner, untested here; the object store's seal file (seal-objects) is written by its own path and was not checked
